spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2022 · General Studies Paper II · Q2
spec.text: “Right of movement and residence throughout the territory of India are freely available to the Indian citizens, but these rights are not absolute.” Comment.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-two. General Studies Paper Two, ten marks, one hundred and fifty words. You know Article nineteen. So why does this answer still lose marks? Let's fix it, line by line.

spec.text: “Right of movement and residence throughout the territory of India are freely available to the Indian citizens, but these rights are not absolute.” Comment.

directives.meaning: give a view, and back it

scenes.vo: Read the last word first. Comment means give your view, and back it. So there are three jobs: the right is free, for citizens. It has limits. And then your verdict, with cases.

spec.stamp: ILLUSTRATIVE · WRITTEN BY US, NOT A CANDIDATE'S COPY

items.text: Article 19(1)(d) and (e) give the right to move freely and to reside and settle anywhere in India.
Article 19(1)(d) and (e) give _citizens_, not foreigners, free movement and residence in India.
These are very important rights in a democracy and they help national unity.
But these rights are not absolute. Article 19(5) allows reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public and to protect Scheduled Tribes.
Thus the rights of movement and residence are not absolute and have restrictions.
What the courts held
• _Gurbachan Singh_ (1952): externment upheld as a reasonable restriction.
• _Ebrahim Vazir Mavat_ (1954): removing a citizen from India violated Article 19(1)(e).
• _Anuradha Bhasin_ (2020): section 144 orders must be necessary and reasoned.
• _Maneka Gandhi_ (1978): these freedoms 'are not and cannot be absolute'.
So the rights are _fundamental yet conditional_: a restriction must be by law, reasonable, and on a named ground.
